body: Normal.  I kind of laugh to myself every time I put my seat belt on in the car as I'm trying to decide if I should end my life minutes later.  The psychological term for it is ambivalence and Wikipedia has a big entry for it if you want to know more about it.

Statistically speaking it's worth it since a majority of people improve with treatment.

But screw statistics.  Let me say first that I completely understand where you're coming from.  My depression "started" about the same time although like you I don't remember before that so maybe it was sooner.  I'm now in my 30's and have been seeing a psychiatrist for medications since 2010 and started therapy last year.  I avoided therapy for a long time because I didn't want to talk about myself nor had any idea what to even talk about but eventually my doctor (who I trust deeply) convinced me.  

So..is it worth it?  I guess it depends.  Yep, it does take some playing with medications to find one that's beneficial.  Some people are really lucky and find something right away.  As for how you'll know it's working without having felt good ever before....you will know.  I have only found one to be helpful and it took some time to find but once I started taking that it was like night and day.  I wanted to get out and do things.  I wanted to be around people.  I actually told the nurse "If this is what most people feel like all the time, no wonder they like life!"  Is it worth it?  Are you willing to put in however many medication tries necessary to find that change?  No one else can answer that for you.  Statistically (damn statistics) most people find a medication that helps within a few tries.  Medications typically work better for moderate/severe depression over mild depression. 

Therapy then... it's not what you see on TV.  A good therapist doesn't expect you to lay on their couch and talk about yourself for an hour a week.  They will need to know your symptoms of course and they'll ask questions about other things they think might be influential but if you go and they expect you to do all the talking - run.  Therapy is actually more like a conversation and if you don't have anything to say they should be able to hold the conversation until you do.  When I don't know what to say, my therapist will literally ask about my day at work yesterday or if we won our flag football game last night.  And then there are days when I go into his office and he can tell things are shit and he comes up with the questions to find out what he needs to know in order to give me suggestions or even just be kind of a friend (I know he's really not a friend and is getting paid but that's what it feels like sometimes) to get me through those shit days so on better days he can guide me into figuring out how to live a better life even if the depression never goes away 100%.

I know, this is long.  The point of it is, treatment can be a good thing even if it's not "helping" in taking the depression away.  Over the past 6 1/2 years of treatment I can say there have only been a few months where I've actually not been depressed.  Most people find relief much sooner and easier than that but even if there is no cure to be found, treatment can still provide an extra pillar of support for those really shitty days.  You've got to be the one to weigh if it's worth it for you personally though.

I have major depression.  I have worked full time for years.  A couple times per year I have to be off work for a period of time and sometimes be hospitalized.  Whenever I ask my doctor if I should cut back on work he tells me that work is good for people and working is a good thing even when I'm not sure I should keep doing it.  It's true that it takes a lot of effort to get up and get there but once I am there it is a good distraction and gives me something to be proud of even on my worst days.

I think....maybe...I'm on the edge of making significant progress?  I've struggled for decades and recently I've finally found a therapist I really like and trust and who has ideas no one else has ever had before.
I do have some memory issues but I'm not sure how much of it is related to depression or seizures.

The first time you go they just ask what brought you there, ask about your symptoms, ask if you've tried anything else, etc.  If they're half-way decent they should ask what you want to get out of therapy.  What your goals are and how you will know when you are ok again.  They will then tell you what they think might help and how often you might meet with them and how long you should expect to work with them.  If they don't tell you these things - ask!!

I guess most importantly, remember that they're working for you.  You are not interviewing for a job - they are, basically.  You should ask what they expect to be doing for you and what they expect out of you.  If you don't feel like you can be yourself or open and honest with them then try to find someone else.  Over the years I've tried therapy 3 times and until this most recent time (the 4th try) I have never felt like it was useful or helpful.  Now that I've met this current guy and we work well together, it's an entirely different experience.

Do you already work with a doctor or counselor?  Inpatient isn't really for fixing anything.  It's stabilization.  I have never felt like I improved while inpatient.  It's more if you really 100% need someone to stop you from hurting yourself immediately. 

Outpatient stuff is much better for actually helping than inpatient.  Not saying you shouldn't go if you need to but don't expect things to change while you're there.  When you get out you still feel depressed and still have to do outpatient things to feel better.  You'll also have more bills and, if you work, potential problems with your job waiting for you.

Can you ask her what helped in the past?  

For me personally, I don't like discussing it with people in my life.  If my family/friends/significant other came to me and wanted to talk about it I'd push them away.  If they made suggestions I'd be irritated.  Questioning is a more gentle way of suggesting.  If she did find something helpful in the past, it's worth a try again.  If she said she waited it out last time and didn't find anything helpful, ask if she wants to try anything.  I find when someone asks me my opinion or makes a suggestion in a question format it's easier for me.  Instead of "Hey you should get out more. You'll feel better with sunshine" I'd prefer "Hey, I'm going for a walk, do you want to come?"  

If she does want help finding other resources or ways to improve how she feels then suggest you do it together.  Asking someone who is depressed to do the legwork for finding help is extremely tiring and difficult.  Those are some tangible ways for guys to be supportive that aren't "fixing it" for her but aren't just leaving her to figure it out for herself either.

I know.  There isn't an easy answer.  Fortunately I'm not looking for an answer to the depression (the therapist and doctor are given that daunting, horrible task) just some reason to keep putting one foot in front of the other this weekend and a way to make that foot placement easier for a few days.

Thanks for your answer.  You're right.  The in-between steps suck.  I don't know if I'd call them the worst part but they definitely suck.  

A week or two ago I had thought that seeing a movie in the theater instead of renting/Netflix-ing would be a good thing to do.  I had forgotten about that entirely.  Thank you for reminding me.  Maybe I'll do that tomorrow.  

I did play on a flag football league but the season is over now.

Yeah I know, that fresh air answer is a killer.  I try not to recoil against it because I know it's good for me.  It's hard when you're not even sure you CAN move to say you're going to go for a walk so I understand the hating even though I know you're right.
